newsitem.title: BULGARIA: Bulgaria Socialists to appeal against opening files.
newsitem.headline: Bulgaria Socialists to appeal against opening files.

text.p: Bulgaria's main opposition Socialists said on Wednesday they would appeal to the Constitutional Court against a new law on the opening of communist-era secret police files.
A spokeswoman for the reformed ex-communist party said it believed the law passed by parliament last week contravened the constitution and violated citizens' rights.

"The law violates the basic principles of division and independence of the state powers, concentrating all the rights in the executive power. It infringes the citizens' right to protection and harms national security," she said.
The law requires police files of top officials including the president, parliamentary deputies, ministers, court officials and state media directors to be made public.

A commission headed by Interior Minister Bogomil Bonev will be set up to check whether the officials worked for the former State Security Service, which the Socialists said would give government authorities power over other state institutions.
The ruling Union of Democratic Forces, which has a clear majority in parliament, has said the law was intended to prevent attempts to blackmail public figures.
Critics of the law say it comes too late, and the more than seven years since the end of communist rule have given ample opportunity for files to be removed or substituted.

Bulgaria's State Security Service was dissolved in 1989 and its files are kept by the interior and defence ministries, the National Intelligence Service and the National Protection Service, which assures security for public figures.
The country's communist secret service, closely allied to the Soviet KGB, had a network of 100,000 agents and informers.
